title: JAMB Arts
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public JAMB UTME arts-subject syllabus. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: The principal told the assembly that the school library would remain open during the holidays so that candidates could revise, and he warned that those who relied only on luck would be disappointed. What reason did the principal give for opening the library?
options: To help candidates revise for their examinations
To sell old books to the students
To punish candidates who came late
To hold a party for the teachers
items.explanation: The principal says the library stays open so candidates can revise and warns against relying on luck, so the reason given is to support revision.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: In the sentence, The chairman was adamant that the meeting must hold today, the word adamant means
items.explanation: Adamant means firmly refusing to change a decision, so it means unwilling to change his mind; confused, tired and eager to cancel contradict the firm stance.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: In the sentence, The new measures were meant to curtail wasteful spending, the word curtail is most nearly opposite in meaning to
items.explanation: Curtail means to cut short or reduce, so its opposite is extend; reduce, control and check are all close in meaning to curtail.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: The teacher wrote a sentence on the board and asked the class to fill the gap. The boys, together with their teacher, ____ already left the hall.
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun boys; the phrase together with their teacher does not change the number, so the plural verb have is correct.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: During the grammar drill the teacher asked the pupils to fill the gap. Neither of the two candidates ____ able to answer the question correctly.
items.explanation: Neither of takes a singular verb even though it refers to two people, so was is correct; were, are and have are all plural forms.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: In the oral English test the examiner asked the class which of the listed words has its primary stress on the second syllable.
items.explanation: Begin is stressed on the second syllable, beGIN, while table, letter and market are all stressed on their first syllable.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: The teacher asked the pupils to identify which of the following words contains a vowel sound different from the others.
items.explanation: Sit, hit and bit all contain the short vowel heard in sit, while seat contains the long vowel heard in see, so seat is the odd one out.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: In the pronunciation drill the class was asked which of the following words begins with a consonant sound different from the others.
items.explanation: Chair, chief and church begin with the ch sound heard in chair, while chemist begins with the k sound heard in kite.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: During the spelling and sound lesson the pupils were asked which of the following words contains a silent letter.
items.explanation: In comb the letter b is not pronounced and is therefore silent, while lamp, hand and tent have no silent letters.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: When the chairman said that the quarrel over seating was a storm in a teacup, he meant that the matter was
items.explanation: A storm in a teacup is an idiom for a great fuss over a trivial matter, so the chairman meant the quarrel was of little importance.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: An elder advised the apprentice that a stitch in time saves nine, meaning that one should
options: wait for other people to solve the problem
avoid hard work whenever it is possible
deal with a problem promptly before it grows
count money carefully before spending it
items.explanation: The proverb means that handling a small problem at once prevents it from growing into a much bigger one, so prompt action is advised.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: Mama Chidi sold her groundnuts in small cups and never raised her price, even when the market was crowded, so buyers always returned to her stall. Why did the buyers always return to her stall?
options: She gave her goods away free of charge
She forced the buyers to buy from her
She only sold to her own relatives
She was fair and consistent in her pricing
items.explanation: She kept her price steady even when demand was high, so her fairness and consistency drew the buyers back rather than any force or free gifts.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: Although the new teacher spoke softly, the pupils listened more carefully than they did to the teacher who often shouted, for they respected her calm authority. What does the passage suggest about the pupils?
options: They responded better to calm authority than to shouting
They disliked all the teachers in the school
They could only hear people who shouted
They were afraid of the new teacher
items.explanation: The pupils listened more carefully to the soft-spoken teacher they respected, which shows they responded better to calm authority than to shouting.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: In the sentence, The witness gave a candid account of the events of that night, the word candid is nearest in meaning to
items.explanation: Candid means honest and straightforward, so frank is nearest in meaning; vague means unclear, which is close to the opposite.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: The teacher asked the pupils to fill the gap in the sentence. Hardly had the bell rung ____ the students rushed out of the hall.
items.explanation: The correlative construction is hardly had ... when, so when is correct; than pairs with no sooner in a different pattern.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Use of English

items.stem: A student reading the line, The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas, was asked to identify the figure of speech used.
items.explanation: The moon is directly called a galleon without using like or as, which is a metaphor; a simile would have used a comparing word.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: In the expression, He fought like a lion, the literary device employed by the writer is
items.explanation: The comparison uses the word like, so it is a simile; a metaphor would state the comparison directly without like or as.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: When a poet describes the wind as whispering to the trees and the flowers as nodding, the figure of speech used is
items.explanation: Giving human actions such as whispering and nodding to the wind and flowers is personification; the other devices do not attribute human behaviour in this way.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: In a play, a character stands alone on the stage and speaks his private thoughts aloud. This speech is called a
items.explanation: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage reveals his inner thoughts; an aside is a brief remark to the audience.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A play that presents the downfall of a person of high rank and ends in disaster is best classified as
items.explanation: A tragedy traces the downfall of a dignified protagonist and ends unhappily, while comedy, farce and satire aim at amusement or correction of folly.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: The chief character in a novel whose actions and fate hold the reader's attention is known as the
items.explanation: The protagonist is the leading character around whom the plot revolves; the antagonist opposes him and the narrator tells the story.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A poem of fourteen lines written in iambic pentameter with a fixed rhyme scheme is called a
items.explanation: A sonnet has fourteen lines with a set rhyme scheme and iambic pentameter; ballads, odes and elegies follow different forms and purposes.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A poem written to mourn the death of a person is known as an
items.explanation: An elegy is a poem of mourning for the dead; an epic is a long heroic narrative, an ode praises a subject, and a lyric expresses personal feeling generally.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: In Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, the protagonist whose life is destroyed by the coming of the white man is
items.explanation: Okonkwo is the central character whose rigid values and tragic end embody the collapse of the old order; Obierika, Unoka and Nwoye are supporting figures.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: In Things Fall Apart, the arrival of the missionaries and the colonial administration chiefly led to
options: the disruption of Igbo communal life and values
the immediate unity of all the clans
the total disappearance of farming among the people
the end of every traditional gathering
items.explanation: The novel shows the missionaries and colonial rule dividing the clan and weakening its customs, so the main effect was disruption of communal life and values.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A novel in which the story is told by the chief character himself, using the pronoun I throughout, is narrated in the
items.explanation: Using I and telling events from the character's own perspective is first-person narration, unlike the omniscient or objective points of view.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: The repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words, as in Peter picked a peck of pickled pepper, is called
items.explanation: Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds, while assonance repeats vowels, onomatopoeia imitates sounds, and rhyme matches end sounds.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A word such as buzz or hiss, which imitates the sound it represents, is an example of
items.explanation: Onomatopoeia is the use of words that imitate natural sounds, so buzz and hiss are examples; the other terms do not describe sound imitation.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: The purging of pity and fear that a tragedy is said to produce in the audience is known as
items.explanation: Catharsis is the emotional release or purging of pity and fear produced by tragedy; hubris is excessive pride and suspense is tense uncertainty.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A novel that traces the growth and development of its main character from childhood to maturity is described as a
items.explanation: A bildungsroman is a coming-of-age story following the protagonist's growth to maturity, unlike an anthology, allegory or parody.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Literature-in-English

items.stem: A constitution whose main provisions are contained in a single document and which can be amended only by a special procedure is described as
items.explanation: A written constitution is codified in one document, and the special amendment process makes it rigid; unwritten constitutions rely on conventions and are flexible.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The principle that no person may be punished except for a clear breach of the law and that all persons are equal before the law is known as
items.explanation: The rule of law holds that government is subject to law and that all citizens are equal before it; the other doctrines describe different political ideas.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: Under the doctrine of separation of powers, the function of making laws is vested in the
items.explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary interprets them, so law-making belongs to the legislature.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: In a federal system of government, governmental powers are constitutionally shared between
options: the central government and the component states
the ruling party and the opposition
items.explanation: Federalism divides powers between a central authority and the constituent states, each supreme in its own sphere, which none of the other pairs describes.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: A system of government in which rulers are periodically chosen through free and fair elections is best described as
items.explanation: Democracy rests on the consent of the governed expressed through regular free elections, whereas autocracy, oligarchy and theocracy rest on one person, a few people or religious authority.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: An organised association whose main aim is to contest elections and control the machinery of government is called a
items.explanation: A political party seeks to win elections and govern, while pressure groups, trade unions and cooperatives seek to influence policy without seeking to govern.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: An organisation that seeks to influence government policy on a particular issue without seeking to govern is best described as a
items.explanation: A pressure group lobbies to influence policy on specific interests but does not contest elections to govern, which distinguishes it from a political party.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The right of adult citizens to vote in public elections is known as
items.explanation: Universal adult suffrage is the right of all adult citizens to vote regardless of status; the other terms relate to law-making, court powers and cabinet conduct.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The body of ministers headed by the president that directs the day-to-day administration of the state is the
items.explanation: The executive implements laws and runs the administration, while the legislature makes laws, the judiciary interprets them and the bureaucracy is the permanent civil service.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The power of the courts to declare an act of the legislature unconstitutional is called
items.explanation: Judicial review is the court's power to test legislation against the constitution; impeachment, filibuster and gerrymandering are unrelated legislative and political tactics.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: Nigeria operates a bicameral national legislature made up of the
options: Senate and the House of Representatives
House of Lords and the House of Commons
National Assembly and the State Assembly
Council of State and the Federal Cabinet
items.explanation: The Nigerian National Assembly is bicameral, consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives; the other options name foreign or non-legislative bodies.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: One lawful way by which a person who was not born in Nigeria may acquire Nigerian citizenship is by
items.explanation: Naturalisation is the legal process by which a foreigner acquires citizenship of a country, while emigration, deportation and extradition concern movement or removal, not acquisition of citizenship.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: A stated objective of the African Union in its Constitutive Act is to
options: impose one single language on all member states
abolish the national governments of member states
promote unity and solidarity among African states
restore colonial administration across the continent
items.explanation: The Constitutive Act lists the promotion of unity and solidarity among African states as a core objective, unlike the other options which contradict its aims.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The document that contains the fundamental rules and principles by which a state is governed is called a
items.explanation: A constitution sets out the fundamental rules and organs of government, whereas a manifesto is a party's programme and the other terms are limited statements of demands or notes.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: The rights to life, personal liberty and fair hearing are examples of
items.explanation: These are fundamental human rights guaranteed by the constitution, while delegated and prerogative powers belong to government and customary duties are obligations, not rights.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Government

items.stem: According to the book of Genesis, God created the heavens, the earth and all living things in six days and rested on the seventh day. Why did God bless and set apart the seventh day?
options: Because it was the first day of creation
Because he rested from all his work of creation
Because the animals were made on that day
Because it was the day people were told to farm
items.explanation: Genesis states that God blessed the seventh day and set it apart because on it he rested from all his work of creation.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: In the Genesis account of creation, God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became
options: the ruler of the skies alone
items.explanation: The text says that when God breathed the breath of life into man he became a living being, distinct from the animals he was given dominion over.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and set the rainbow in the cloud as
options: a warning that floods would come every year
a lamp to light the earth at night
a law for the builders of the ark
a sign of the covenant between God and the earth
items.explanation: God set the rainbow in the cloud as the sign of his covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, not as a warning or law.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: God called Abram to leave his country and promised to make of him a great nation and to bless him, so that in him
options: all the families of the earth would be blessed
all the nations of the earth would be destroyed
the land of Egypt would be given to him
the tower of Babel would be rebuilt
items.explanation: In the call of Abram, God promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, a promise repeated in the covenant.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: God chose Moses to lead the Israelites out of Egypt, and when Pharaoh repeatedly refused to release them God sent
options: an army of Israelites into Egypt
a prophet to Egypt from Rome
items.explanation: Because Pharaoh hardened his heart, God sent ten plagues upon Egypt before he allowed the Israelites to leave.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: At Mount Sinai, God gave Moses the Ten Commandments, which were written
options: on the wall of the temple
items.explanation: The commandments were written by God on two stone tablets and given to Moses on Mount Sinai, as recorded in Exodus.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: When Jesus was asked which commandment was the greatest, he said one should love the Lord with all the heart, soul and mind, and that the second was to
options: offer sacrifice at the temple daily
give all goods to the priests
items.explanation: Jesus named love of God first and said the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself, on which all the law and prophets hang.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: A teacher explaining the parable of the Good Samaritan stressed that Jesus told it in order to teach that a person's neighbour is
options: anyone in need, regardless of tribe or religion
only the member of one's own family
only the person who lives next door
only the priest who serves at the temple
items.explanation: The Samaritan helped a wounded stranger from another community, so Jesus taught that a neighbour is anyone in need, whatever his tribe or religion.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: In the parable of the Prodigal Son, the father welcomed, embraced and forgave the returning son, an act that chiefly shows
options: the father's fear of the elder son
God's readiness to forgive a repentant sinner
the son's right to a second inheritance
that hard work is never rewarded
items.explanation: The father's joyful welcome of the repentant son portrays God's willingness to forgive those who return to him, even when others resent it.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: When Jesus was tempted by Satan in the wilderness, he answered each temptation by
options: calling upon the Pharisees for help
performing a miracle to silence Satan
quoting the word of God from the scriptures
items.explanation: At each temptation Jesus replied with words from the scriptures, showing reliance on the word of God rather than on miracles or escape.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: A Bible study group discussed the Sermon on the Mount and noted that Jesus pronounced the meek, the merciful and the peacemakers to be
options: the rulers of the earth in that age
the enemies of the kingdom of heaven
the people who would surely perish
blessed and called children of God
items.explanation: In the Beatitudes Jesus declared such people blessed, and he called the peacemakers sons of God, that is, children of God.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and Peter preached, with the result that about three thousand people
options: were baptised and added to the church
asked that the temple be rebuilt
items.explanation: After Peter's sermon at Pentecost about three thousand souls were baptised and joined the early Christian community, as recorded in Acts.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: Saul of Tarsus, who had persecuted the early church, was dramatically converted to Christianity on the road to
items.explanation: The book of Acts records that Saul was confronted by the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and was converted there.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: In his letters, Paul taught that Christians are members of one body, and he drew from this the lesson that
options: only the leaders matter in the church
members should compete with one another for honour
every member is important and should be cared for
the weak members should be cast out
items.explanation: Paul compared the church to a body whose many members need one another, teaching that every member is valuable and worthy of care.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies

items.stem: The early Christian community in Jerusalem sold their possessions and shared what they had with all who were in need, and this showed
options: the desire of the believers to become rich
disagreement over who should lead them
generosity and unity among the believers
items.explanation: Acts describes the believers holding all things in common and distributing to each as any had need, which demonstrates generosity and unity.
items.reference: JAMB UTME Syllabus - Christian Religious Studies
